title: Great is your faith (Matthew 15:21–39)
hookLine: left on read, she asks again, shorter, and finds room in his own words
tomorrow: how does one sour comment take over a whole group?

cards: Left on read. The three dots appear, then vanish. So you ask again, shorter this time.
A woman in Matthew knows that silence. She's from Canaan, from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel, and her daughter is suffering.

She follows Jesus and his friends down the road, calling out: "Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou son of David." Then a line that stops the scene cold: "But he answered her not a word." The disciples want her gone.

teach.h: NOT A WORD, THEN NOT SENT.
teach.b: His first answer is about his mission: "I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel."

She comes closer, kneels, and makes her request shorter: "Lord, help me." His second answer is harder still: "It is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it to dogs." These are difficult words to hear.
Some readers take them as a test of her; some hear Jesus' mission widening, right there in the conversation. Matthew doesn't say which. What Matthew does show is her answer.
She doesn't argue with the picture.

teach.h: YET THE DOGS EAT OF THE CRUMBS.
teach.b: She steps inside it: "Truth, Lord: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table." Bread, a table, crumbs. She takes his own image and finds room in it for her daughter.

teach.h: O WOMAN, GREAT IS THY FAITH.
teach.b: And this time he answers her fully: "O woman, great is thy faith: be it unto thee even as thou wilt." Her daughter is made whole from that very hour. Notice who gets the praise.

Not a disciple. A mother from outside, who kept asking, each time shorter and plainer. Then Matthew moves on to a hillside where a crowd is fed from seven loaves, and baskets of broken pieces are left over.
Right after she asks for crumbs.

how: Some Christians keep a prayer list of people they ask for again and again, and some churches read the Canaanite woman's story as a picture of persistent prayer.

games.q: what does “great is your faith” mean?
o: praise for a mother who wouldn't stop asking
praise for a disciple who walked on water
a blessing said over every child in Israel

games.q: she keeps asking — tap the pairs.

s: "But he answered her not a word."
the disciples asked him to send her away
they said, send her away; for she crieth after us.
she argued that his picture of bread and dogs was wrong
she stepped inside it: yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' table.

games.q: you've asked your manager twice for a schedule change so you can drive your mom to treatment. no answer. what fits the woman in Matthew 15?
o: write one long email with every reason at once.
ask again, in person, shorter and plainer.
games.why: met with silence, she kept asking, each time shorter: have mercy, Lord, help me, then the crumbs. and Jesus said, great is thy faith.

practice: Write by hand the name of someone you keep asking for, for healing, for a job, for a way back. Her words, Lord, help me, are short enough to write beside the name. Look at the two together while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Great is your faith. What Jesus says to a Canaanite mother who wouldn't stop asking, and who found room for her daughter in his own words.

orig.note: Greek of Matthew 15:28: great is your faith.

carryVoice: Your line: great is your faith, said to someone who simply kept asking. Rest easy.
